attribution.note: Marcus describes and endorses his own testing experience.

semantics.note: The proposition preserves the first correct answer and subsequent errors within his own session.

contract.note: The contract strengthens many errors into errors on most subsequent prompts. That majority threshold is unwarranted, although the missing independent session record leaves either reading unresolved.

reviews.rationale: The packet contains no independent evidence of the specific session. Marcus's account cannot establish its own accuracy. The absence of corroboration does not contradict him or make the case broken.

attribution.note: This is Marcus's own assessment of Deep Search.

semantics.note: The normalisation preserves his expressly tentative impression and qualitative frequency.

contract.note: The contract turns a hedged impression into a measurable frequency claim. The plain-reading allowance applies only to firm language and cannot authorize scoring this hedge.

evidence.note: An independent, pre-cutoff report, but its news-identification task does not measure subtle errors in DeepSearch reports.
The researchers discuss confidence across search tools, without measuring error detection in Grok 3 DeepSearch reports.

reviews.rationale: Marcus qualifies the claimed error frequency as an impression. Policy excludes hedged claims from scoring. The supplied citation-task evidence also does not establish the asserted DeepSearch report characteristics.

attribution.note: Marcus states this observation in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition preserves the contemporaneous valuation trend and its temporary qualification. It does not establish a causal claim about valuation drivers.

contract.note: Reading valuations as those of leading private AI labs around the post is ordinary in context. The contract explicitly permits reported funding talks; the evaluative aside about results is not scored.

evidence.note: Reuters reports February talks valuing xAI at about $75 billion versus a prior $40 billion. These are reported negotiations, not a completed round.
Reuters reports OpenAI's proposed pre-money valuation at $260 billion versus a prior $150 billion. The $300 billion headline includes proposed new funds.
This company disclosure concerns a March 3 round, outside the historical target period. It is available before evaluation but cannot establish the earlier trend.

reviews.rationale: Within the contract's ordinary private-lab reading, contemporaneous reports place both xAI and OpenAI above their previous valuations. Funding talks satisfy the stated criteria. The packet's public-stock caveat concerns a different metric, and no claim about whether results justified valuations is established.

attribution.note: Marcus endorses both the factual assertion and the accompanying warning.

semantics.note: The central assertion is observational. The accompanying recommendation to beware is normative and should not itself receive an empirical grade.

contract.note: The contract allows frequent missed errors to satisfy a claim about errors most people would miss. Those quantities are not interchangeable; the plain-reading allowance does not erase the explicit majority-of-people scope.

evidence.note: The study tested assistants in December 2024, despite the item's February event label. It supports common output problems, but significant issues include more than factual errors and it does not measure user detection.

Supports frequent programming-answer errors and substantial missed misinformation. Missing errors 39% of the time does not establish that most people miss subtle errors, nor directly contradict that assertion.
The report is available before evaluation, but the packet does not establish testing by February 19. Its assessment of confident tone also supplies no measured majority-of-users detection rate.

reviews.rationale: Independent studies support frequent errors in tested domains and users overlooking some polished misinformation. They do not settle whether subtle errors would escape most people. The 39% figure measures missed-error occasions, not the claimed population majority. The full assertion remains unresolved.
